title: Let’s Take a Look at Space Cadets Away Missions
body:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=acvpoQwncqI

Daniel (@dungeondive) opens with a recommendation for X Minus One, the 1950s radio series that adapted Golden Age science fiction and shaped his imagination long before he read the source material, then explains why revisiting it sent him back to Space Cadets: Away Missions (Stronghold Games, 2015). His argument is that this is a forgotten game that accomplishes a great deal with modest components. The rulebook is one of the best he knows, full of repetition, pictures and an extended play example, and the mission book offers a stack of scenarios nearly all playable with two to six rocketeers.

The design lesson is the overkill system. Attacks roll d10s where 1 to 3 succeed; the first success is a hit and every extra one is an overkill to spend on an effect tied to your weapon, your character, your IQ check or even the alien you just killed. He wonders aloud why more dungeon crawlers have not stolen it. Oxygen doubles as a spendable pool of extra actions you can never fully drain, mind-slaved human thralls must be subdued rather than shot, and scanning reveals more aliens the more players you bring.

The back half turns to vintage anthologies: Anthony Boucher's Treasury of Great Science Fiction, the Playboy collections, Frederik Pohl's Star series, and a reading of the opening of Bester's The Stars My Destination, which he calls ground zero for cyberpunk.

----

Daniel says the overkill system should have been copied by every dungeon crawler since. Which mechanism from an overlooked game do you wish had become standard?
